tweet.text:
After guiding Claude through a few refactorings I asked it an interesting and pertinent question.  I got a very interesting, if predictable, answer.

❯ do refactorings like this help you (Claude) read the code?

⏺ Yes, genuinely. A few specific ways:
1. Named intent - When I see army-adjacent-to-enemy-city? in a call site, I understand what's
being checked without reading the implementation. With the inline version, I had to parse the
some over neighbor-offsets checking hostile-city? to understand the purpose.
2. Reduced working memory - Nested cond/let/if expressions require me to hold multiple levels
of context. When set-attention-message had the cargo logic, reason logic, and damage logic all
inline, I had to mentally track more state to understand any single part.
3. Comments as anchors - The comments like "Returns cargo description for units that carry
other units" let me skip reading the implementation when I'm trying to understand the caller.
4. Predictable structure - case and simple when have obvious control flow. A 5-branch cond with
nested 3-branch cond inside requires more careful tracing.
That said, I can parse complex nested code - it's not a hard limit. But I'm more likely to make
reasoning errors with deeply nested logic, the same way humans are. The refactored versions
let me build understanding incrementally: understand cargo-string, then understand how it's
used, rather than understanding everything at once.
The cyclomatic complexity metric roughly tracks "number of paths I need to consider" - and
fewer paths means fewer chances to miss an edge case when reasoning about behavior.
